title: Bull and bear spreads
objectives: Build a spread from two strikes and read its capped payoff.
Find a spread's net cost, maximum profit and break-even.

screens.prose: You buy a call struck at £100.00 and, at the same time, sell a call struck at £110.00. Both expire on the same day. The dashed line rising to the right is the bought call; the one falling is the sold call. The bold line is the pair.
screens.question: The share ends at £118.00. What does the pair pay you at expiry?

widget.label: Payoff of the pair
widget.accept: £10.00: £18.00 from the bought call less £8.00 owed on the sold one

hints.text: Work out each call on its own, then add the two.
The call you sold is exercised against you above £110.00.
The bought call pays £18.00. On the sold call you hand over £8.00. Together that is £10.00.

feedback.correct: £18.00 from the bought call, less £8.00 owed on the sold one.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find each call's payoff at £118.00, with the sold one counted against you.

byKey.long-only: You counted the call you bought but not the one you sold. Its buyer exercises and takes £8.00 back.
byKey.added: You added the sold call's £8.00. That payoff belongs to its buyer, so it comes off yours.
byKey.sold-only: You counted only the sold call. The bought call pays you £18.00 as well.

explain.text: The bought call pays $118 - 100 = 18$. The call you sold is exercised against you, costing $118 - 110 = 8$. Together they pay £10.00.

screens.prose: Slide the price at expiry from left to right and watch the bold line. Its label shows what the pair pays.
screens.question: Above which price does the payoff stop rising?

options.text: £110.00, the strike of the call you sold
£100.00, the strike of the call you bought
options.why: That is where the payoff starts rising. Slide on: it climbs £1.00 a pound up to £110.00.
You followed the dashed line of the bought call. Above £110.00 the sold call takes back every extra pound.

hints.text: Compare the payoff at £112.00 and at £120.00.
Look at what happens to the right of the sold strike.

feedback.correct: Above £110.00, every extra pound the bought call earns, the sold call gives back.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide the price above £110.00 and compare two prices there.

explain.text: Between the strikes only the bought call pays, so the line climbs. Above £110.00 the two calls move together and cancel. The payoff is capped at $110 - 100 = 10$.

screens.prose: A long call with a short call at a higher strike is a **bull call spread**. It gains when the share rises. You paid £6.00 for the £100.00 call. You received £2.50 for the £110.00 call.
screens.question: What does the spread cost you today, in total?

hints.text: Which premium did you pay, and which did you receive?
Selling a call brings money in.
You pay £6.00 and receive £2.50, so take one from the other.

feedback.correct: £6.00 out, £2.50 in: a net cost of £3.50.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count money paid as a cost and money received as income.

byKey.added: You added the two premiums. You received the £2.50, so it comes off the £6.00.
byKey.bought: That is the bought call alone. Selling the other call brought in £2.50.
byKey.sold: That is what you received. You also paid £6.00 for the bought call.

explain.text: The premium you receive pays for part of the one you buy. The net cost of £3.50 is the spread's **net debit**. The profit line is the payoff line moved down by it.

screens.prose: Fill in the table leg by leg. A sold call's payoff is negative when it is exercised against you. Profit is the spread's payoff less the £3.50 net cost.
screens.question: Complete the payoff table for the £100.00/£110.00 bull call spread.

hints.text: Do each call on its own, then add across the row.
Only the bottom row is above the sold strike.
At £120.00: +20 from the bought call, −10 from the sold one. The payoff is 10 and the profit is 10 − 3.50 = 6.50.

feedback.correct: The payoff never passes £10.00, and the profit never passes £6.50.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Fill each call's payoff first, then add, then take off £3.50.

byKey.r0c4: Below both strikes nothing pays, so you are down the whole net cost: −3.50.
byKey.r1c4: Profit is payoff less the net cost: 5.00 − 3.50.
byKey.r2c3: At £110.00 the bought call pays 10 and the sold call is not yet exercised.
byKey.r3c2: The buyer of your £110.00 call exercises at £120.00. You hand over £10.00, so write −10.
byKey.r3c3: Add across: 20 from the bought call and −10 from the sold one.

explain.text: Below £100.00 you lose the £3.50 you paid. Between the strikes the profit climbs £1.00 a pound. Above £110.00 it sits at £6.50, the **maximum profit**: the £10.00 cap less the net cost.

screens.prose: Now move the strike of the call you sell. A call with a higher strike is worth less, so it brings in less premium. The caption shows that premium, the net cost and the cap.

derive.caption: Sold call brings in {{money(premium.c2)}}. Net cost {{money(6 - premium.c2)}}. Cap {{money(strike.c2 - 100)}}.

screens.question: What happens as you raise the upper strike?

options.text: The net cost rises and the cap rises
The net cost falls and the cap rises
options.why: You kept the sold call's premium fixed. A higher strike sells for less, so less comes in and the spread costs more.

options.text: The net cost rises and the cap falls
options.why: The cap is the gap between the strikes. Raising the upper strike widens that gap.

hints.text: Try £104.00 and then £118.00, and read the caption each time.
The cap is the gap between the two strikes.
At £104.00 the spread costs £1.77 with a £4.00 cap. At £118.00 it costs £4.76 with an £18.00 cap.

feedback.correct: A wider spread keeps more of the rise, and you pay more for it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the net cost and the cap at two different strikes.

explain.text: A wider spread keeps more of the rise, so it costs more. A narrow one is cheap but capped early. With the upper strike far away, the spread becomes the bought call alone.

screens.prose: Back to the £100.00/£110.00 spread, at a net cost of £3.50. One colleague says it breaks even at £100.00, where the bought call starts to pay. Another adds the £6.00 and £2.50 premiums to the lower strike.
screens.question: At what share price at expiry does the spread break even?

widget.label: Break-even price
widget.accept: £103.50: the lower strike plus the £3.50 net cost

hints.text: How far must the payoff climb to win back the net cost?
Between the strikes the payoff is $S_T - 100$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find where the payoff equals the net cost you paid.

byKey.lower: You took the lower strike. At £100.00 the spread pays nothing, and you are down the £3.50 you paid.
byKey.added: You added the two premiums. The £2.50 you received offsets the £6.00 you paid, so only £3.50 must come back.
byKey.gross: You won back the £6.00 you paid but forgot the £2.50 you received.

explain.text: The payoff must reach the net cost, £3.50. Between the strikes it is $S_T - 100$, so $S_T = 103.50$. The break-even sits above the lower strike by the net cost.

screens.prose: Now the version for a fall. On another share, buy a put struck at £50.00 for £4.00. Sell a put struck at £45.00 for £1.50. This is a **bear put spread**.
screens.question: Fill in the spread's key numbers.

hints.text: Mirror what you did for calls: net the premiums, then find the cap.
The payoff stops growing below the sold strike, £45.00.

feedback.correct: Net cost £2.50, cap £5.00, maximum profit £2.50, break-even £47.50.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Net the premiums, find the cap, then the break-even below the upper strike.

byKey.r0c1: You paid £4.00 and received £1.50. Net them.
byKey.r1c1: The payoff stops growing at the sold strike. The cap is the gap between the strikes.
byKey.r2c1: Maximum profit is the £5.00 cap less the £2.50 net cost.
byKey.r3c1: A put spread gains as the price falls. Start at the upper strike, £50.00, and go down by the net cost.

explain.text: The bear put spread is the bull call spread turned round. It is capped below the sold strike and breaks even at $50 - 2.50 = 47.50$. The most you can lose is the £2.50 you paid.

screens.prose: Back to the £100.00/£110.00 call spread. The diamond on the price axis is the strike of the call you sold. Drag it and watch the bold payoff line.
screens.question: Drag the sold call's strike until the spread pays £0.00 at every price.

hints.text: The payoff climbs only between the two strikes.
Close the gap between the strikes.
Put the sold strike on top of the bought one, at £100.00.

feedback.correct: Equal strikes: every pound the bought call pays, the sold call takes back.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at where the payoff climbs, and make that stretch vanish.

byKey.below: You went past it. Now the sold call pays out first, so the payoff is negative above £100.00.
byKey.apart: The strikes are still apart, so the line still climbs between them.

explain.text: With both strikes at £100.00 the two calls cancel at every price, and so do their premiums. Push the sold strike below the bought one and you receive more than you pay. That is a **credit spread**, which profits if the share does not rise.

screens.prose: You built the spread leg by leg. With strikes $K_1 < K_2$ and net cost $D$, the payoff is $$\max(S_T - K_1, 0) - \max(S_T - K_2, 0).$$ It is capped at $K_2 - K_1$. The maximum profit is $K_2 - K_1 - D$ and the break-even is $K_1 + D$.
screens.question: A bull call spread uses strikes £60.00 and £70.00 and costs £4.00 net. Where does it break even?

options.why: That is the lower strike. There the spread pays nothing and you are down £4.00.
You came down from the upper strike. A call spread gains as the price rises, so go up from the lower strike.
You added the net cost to the upper strike. Above £70.00 the payoff is already capped.

explain.text: From the lower strike the payoff climbs £1.00 a pound. It reaches the £4.00 net cost at £64.00. The maximum profit is $10 - 4 = 6$.

screens.prose: Now prove the break-even rule for any bull call spread with strikes $K_1 < K_2$ and net cost $D$, where $0 < D < K_2 - K_1$.
screens.question: Put the lines of the argument in order.

lines.text: Below $K_1$ neither call pays, so profit is $-D < 0$: no break-even there.
Between the strikes only the bought call pays, so the payoff is $S_T - K_1$.
Profit is payoff less the net cost: $S_T - K_1 - D$.
Setting the profit to 0 gives $S_T = K_1 + D$, which lies between the strikes since $D < K_2 - K_1$.

hints.text: Start by ruling out the region where nothing pays.
The middle region is where the profit changes.
Rule out below $K_1$, write the payoff between the strikes, subtract $D$, then solve.

feedback.correct: Each line uses the one before it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Rule out the low prices first, then build the profit and solve.

explain.text: Below $K_1$ the profit is stuck at $-D$. Between the strikes it is $S_T - K_1 - D$, which is 0 at $K_1 + D$. The condition $D < K_2 - K_1$ keeps that point below the cap.

screens.prose: A fund expects a share at £100.00 to rally modestly after earnings, to about £108.00. It does not believe in a move past £110.00. So it sells that upside to fund the call: the spread at £3.50, not the £100.00 call alone at £6.00.
screens.question: Below what price at expiry does the spread make more than the call alone?

hints.text: Above £110.00 the spread's profit is flat. Where does the call's profit reach it?
Above £100.00 the call alone makes $S_T - 106$.

feedback.correct: Only above £112.50 does the call alone do better.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Set the call's profit equal to the spread's £6.50 cap.

byKey.cap: At £110.00 the spread makes £6.50 and the call only £4.00. The call needs more rise to catch up.
byKey.be: You added the net cost to the upper strike. Compare the two profits instead.
byKey.callbe: That is the call's own break-even. There the spread is already £2.50 ahead.

explain.text: Below £110.00 the spread is always £2.50 ahead, the premium it collected. At £108.00 it makes £4.50 against £2.00. Only above $106 + 6.50 = 112.50$ does the call win, a move the fund does not expect.

ideas: A bull call spread buys a call and sells one at a higher strike. The premium received cuts the cost.
The payoff is capped at the gap between the strikes. Maximum profit is that gap less the net cost.
The break-even is the lower strike plus the net cost. A bear put spread mirrors it with puts.

formula.name: Bull call spread
formula.note: Capped at $K_2 - K_1$; break-even at $K_1 + D$.

summary.trap: Adding the premiums instead of netting them, or putting the break-even at the lower strike. It sits at $K_1$ plus the net cost.

quiz.prose: A bull call spread: buy the £50.00 call for £3.00 and sell the £55.00 call for £1.20.
quiz.question: Where does it break even at expiry?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Net the premiums, then add to the lower strike.

byKey.lower: You took the lower strike. There the spread pays nothing.
byKey.added: You added the premiums. The £1.20 you receive comes off the £3.00.
byKey.gross: You added only the bought call's premium. The sold call brought in £1.20.

explain.text: The net cost is $3.00 - 1.20 = 1.80$. Between the strikes the payoff is $S_T - 50$, which reaches 1.80 at £51.80.

quiz.prose: The same £50.00/£55.00 bull call spread, at a net cost of £1.80.
quiz.question: What is its maximum profit?

widget.label: Maximum profit
widget.accept: £3.20: the £5.00 cap less the £1.80 net cost

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the net cost off the most the spread can pay.

byKey.payoff: That is the maximum payoff. Profit takes off the £1.80 you paid.
byKey.cost: That is the net cost, the most you can lose.
byKey.added: You took off both premiums added together. Net them first.

explain.text: The payoff is capped at $55 - 50 = 5$. Taking off the net cost leaves $5 - 1.80 = 3.20$.

quiz.prose: You **sell** the £100.00 call for £6.00 and **buy** the £110.00 call for £2.50. The short strike is now below the long one.
quiz.question: What is this position, and what is its worst loss at expiry?

options.text: A bull call spread; worst loss £3.50
options.why: You read the legs the usual way round. Here you sold the lower strike, so you gain if the share stays down.
£3.50 is what you receive. Above £110.00 you owe the £10.00 gap, less that £3.50.

options.text: A credit spread; it cannot lose, as you are paid upfront
options.why: Being paid first does not cap the payout. Above £100.00 the sold call is exercised against you.

feedback.correct: You collect £3.50 and can owe up to £10.00.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out what you receive today and what you owe above £110.00.

explain.text: You receive $6.00 - 2.50 = 3.50$ today. Above £110.00 you owe $110 - 100 = 10$. The worst case is $10 - 3.50 = 6.50$.

quiz.prose: A trader expects a share at £100.00 to end near £106.00, and not above £110.00.
quiz.question: Why might they prefer the £100.00/£110.00 call spread at £3.50 to the £100.00 call alone at £6.00?

options.text: It costs less, and it gives up only gains above £110.00 that they do not expect
It has a higher maximum profit than the call
options.why: The call alone has no cap. The spread's maximum is £6.50.

options.text: It breaks even lower because the premiums add up
options.why: It breaks even lower because the premiums net, not add: £103.50 against £106.00.

feedback.correct: The trader sells the upside they do not believe in.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare what each costs and what each gives up.

explain.text: The spread costs £2.50 less and breaks even at £103.50, not £106.00. It gives up only gains above £110.00. At £106.00 it makes £2.50 where the call makes nothing.
